look_here_first: Start at the BASE and LEAVES: a tufted perennial with very narrow, inward-rolled (involute) blades. Confirm by viewing the cross section of a fresh, mature leaf. Then examine the often still OPEN but relatively fine/less-showy panicle; do not claim this species has a closed inflorescence. Narrow blades alone are not a species-level diagnosis.

project_inclusion.range_basis: Hays — Master Plant Pool Hays-local source. Williamson — UT Plant Resources Center county flora includes Eragrostis lugens. Bell — Hagenbuch & Lemke Hill Country grass treatment cites a Bell County voucher.

best_field_traits: leaf blades very narrow, about 1–2 mm wide
panicle less extravagantly spreading than E. spectabilis
morphology_keys.comparison_training: E. lugens has the narrowest, firmest, most involute foliage of this B094 set. E. secundiflora shows clustered spikelets along panicle branches; E. spectabilis forms a much broader airy purple panicle.
morphology_keys.field_teaching_note: Kew/GrassBase describes lugens as a perennial with 1–2 mm blades, an open ovate/pyramidal panicle, and small spikelets about 3–4.5 mm long with several florets. Many pressed stems alone cannot prove the blade is naturally involute.
morphology_keys.crew_recognition_summary: MOURNING LOVEGRASS = unusually thin leaves and airy but finer panicle. Confirm inward-rolled blade with live cross section.
what_to_photograph_for_confirmation: Live rooted mature plant (not just a herbarium specimen).
Fresh blade cross-section at 10–20× to confirm involute margins.
Collar, sheath mouth and true ligule macro with ruler.
Mature panicle branch and 2–3 spikelets beside a millimeter scale.

comparisons.key_distinctions: E. intermedia and E. spectabilis may form similarly wispy panicles. Narrow, firm, inward-rolled mature leaves and correctly dissected spikelets help separate E. lugens; E. secundiflora has conspicuously crowded, large spikelets, unlike lugens. Similar dropseeds (Sporobolus) differ at individual floret/spikelet architecture; do not use panicle shape alone.

field_photo_quickcheck.heading: Eragrostis lugens — follow the real-photo field cues
steps: See the very narrow mostly green-to-straw blades, and look for a persistent tufted base.

In the second archived Texas herbarium photograph, the lower-left pressed clump actually shows fibrous roots. The new root arrow is a visible structure, NOT proof of a living perennial crown, connected rhizomes, or that all detached flowering stalks belong to one individual.
Inspect a mature FRESH blade edge with 10× magnification; rolling must be observable, NOT inferred from a pressed herbarium strip.
The mature panicle can be wispy/open too; check isolated multi-flowered spikelets and compare with E. intermedia and E. spectabilis.
field_photo_quickcheck.field_rule: MOURNING LOVEGRASS = unusually thin leaves and airy but finer panicle. Confirm inward-rolled blade with live cross section.
field_photo_quickcheck.warning: Current locally saved pictures are PRESSSED HERBARIUM SHEETS from two different Texas voucher records. Arrows may indicate visible blade strips, spread flowering branches and the specimen clump, but cannot confirm an involute cross-section or exact ligule anatomy. These sheets also show the panicle is not necessarily contracted.

measured_diagnostic_key.evidence_scope: Published GrassBase morphology; measurements not inferred from existing herbarium photos.
measured_diagnostic_key.blades: Mature blades 8–20 cm × 1–2 mm, often involute; verify fresh cross-section.
measured_diagnostic_key.collar: Sheath mouth hairy; ligule fringe of hairs. Photograph with mm scale.
measured_diagnostic_key.panicle: Open, about 18–28 cm long; not necessarily contracted.
measured_diagnostic_key.glumes: Lower about 0.6–1 mm, upper 1.1–1.4 mm; one-veined.
measured_diagnostic_key.lemma: Approximately 1.5–1.6 mm, three-veined; inspect palea keels.
measured_diagnostic_key.awn: Do not infer awn character from pressed vouchers.
measured_diagnostic_key.comparison: E. intermedia, E. spectabilis and E. secundiflora require mature spikelet comparisons; Sporobolus typically has one floret per spikelet.
